messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Sara, a 23-year-old South Eastern Asian woman who works as a ship captain, has sought help for her ongoing struggles with anxiety and fear. Her journey began in childhood when she experienced physical abuse at the hands of a caregiver, an experience that left deep psychological scars. Sara had come to believe that the world was inherently dangerous, and this belief only intensified over time. Nighttime and darkness were particularly triggering for Sara; they reminded her of those frightening moments from her childhood when she felt most vulnerable. As soon as night fell, she would feel a surge of tension in her body, ready at any moment to react to danger. The dark was more than just the absence of light—it represented an echo of the fear and helplessness that had defined those early years. Driving with others also triggered Sara’s anxiety, especially when men were involved. She found herself constantly monitoring their behavior, always on edge, expecting something bad to happen. Her body would tighten in anticipation, and she felt like she was walking a tightrope, one false move away from disaster. This constant state of alertness made her wary of any situation that brought her close to other people. Sara had come to believe that the world was indeed dangerous and that she was fundamentally defective. She felt isolated and set apart from others, as though they couldn’t understand what she went through or why she acted the way she did. This sense of isolation often led to more triggers. For instance, being alone with men heightened her fear because it reminded her of those painful past experiences. Sara’s ship captain role also became a source of significant stress. She dreaded having male crew members as part of her team, always planning escape routes and feeling tense whenever she had to interact with them closely. The combination of her job responsibilities and her need for safety often put her in situations where her anxiety spiraled out of control. This constant threat monitoring not only affected her work but also strained her relationships. What frightened Sara most was the idea that these fears might never subside, that she would always be on edge, constantly looking over her shoulder. She had become convinced that there was something fundamentally wrong with her—that this state of hyper-vigilance and fear was a part of who she was. This belief reinforced her triggers, making it difficult for her to feel safe in any situation. The turning point came when Sara realized that her fears were starting to take over her life completely. She no longer enjoyed the parts of her job that once brought her joy, and her social life had dwindled to almost nothing. It was this realization that finally pushed her to seek help. What she most hoped for was a chance to break free from these relentless thoughts and feelings—to reclaim some sense of normalcy and peace in her daily life. In seeking therapy, Sara is looking for the tools to manage her anxiety and find ways to live without being consumed by constant fear. She hopes that with support, she can rebuild her confidence and reconnect with others, breaking the cycle that has kept her isolated and anxious for so long.
